items.body: AI training and inference create sudden load changes that stress cooling and electrical systems, leading to hardware failures.
items.whyImportant: If true, AI data centers face higher maintenance costs and reduced operational reliability.

items.title: Local grid instability
items.body: Erratic power draw from AI clusters causes voltage fluctuations on local grids, increasing the risk of blackouts and power quality issues.
items.whyImportant: This could restrict AI data center siting, favoring locations with robust grid infrastructure and advanced power management.

evidence.title: Pending verification for grid impact
evidence.description: Primary source still under verification; dossier context note highlights potential grid strain.

pattern.title: From capacity to volatility
pattern.before: The AI infrastructure race focused narrowly on securing megawatt-scale power capacity to meet growing compute demand.
pattern.shift: Emerging evidence suggests that the volatility of AI power draw—not just total consumption—is damaging equipment and destabilizing grids.
pattern.now: The binding constraint is shifting from pure capacity to power-quality and grid-stability limits.
pattern.conclusion: Addressing AI energy needs will require not only more power but also advanced power conditioning, resilient grid infrastructure, and siting strategies that account for load volatility.

insight.title: AI power volatility reshapes infrastructure requirements
insight.formula: AI infrastructure reliability = f(power quality, not just quantity)
insight.explanation: The assumption that abundant megawatts suffice for AI growth is challenged by evidence that rapid load swings cause physical harm and instability, making power conditioning and local grid robustness equally critical.
